'''''Gomphocarpus physocarpus''''' is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the Milkweed subfamily, [[Asclepiadoideae]], and Dogbane Family [[Apocynaceae]].<ref name=POWO>{{cite taxon |POWO |id=97670-1 |title=''Gomphocarpus physocarpus'' E.Mey. |access-date=June 20, 2026}}</ref><ref name=COL>{{Catalogue of Life |id= 6KQ43 |title=''Gomphocarpus physocarpus'' E.Mey. |access-date=June 20, 2026}}</ref> It is commonly known as '''hairy balls''', '''balloonplant''', '''balloon cotton-bush''', '''bishop's balls''', '''nailhead''', or '''swan plant'''.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Mahr |first1=Susan |title=Balloon Plant, Gomphocarpus physocarpus |url=https://hort.extension.wisc.edu/articles/balloon-plant-gomphocarpus-physocarpus/ |website=Wisconsin Horticulture |publisher=University of Wisconsin-Madison |access-date=4 September 2023}}</ref> The plant is native to southeast Africa, but it has been widely naturalised as it is often used as an ornamental plant.

==Description==
[[File:Monarch Butterfly Caterpillars.JPG|left|thumb|160px|[[Monarch butterfly]] caterpillars feeding on ''Gomphocarpus physocarpus'']]
''Gomphocarpus physocarpus'' is an undershrub perennial herb, that can grow to {{cvt|2|m}} tall with narrow [[lanceolate]] leaves. The plant blooms in warm months. It grows on roadside banks, at altitudes of {{cvt|850|–|1500|m}} above sea level. The plant prefers moderate moisture, as well as sandy and well-drained soil and full sun.

Its propagation can be done by seeds or by cuttings. The seeds can be sown in a light, well-drained substrate. Cuttings about 10 cm long with the basal leaves removed can be planted in a pot with light, well-draining substrate.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Agronamidia |first=Redação |date=2023-10-06 |title=Planta balão: a beleza e a curiosidade de uma planta exótica |url=https://agronamidia.com.br/paisagismo/planta-balao/ |access-date=2025-07-26 |language=pt-BR}}</ref>

''Gomphocarpus physocarpus'' is traditionally used to produce ointments for the treatment of warts and the seeds are used in rituals. The leaves and stems produce milky latex that contains carbohydrates, cardiac glycosides (cardenolides), terpenoids, alkaloids, and phenols.<ref>Munsamy, A., & Naidoo, Y. (2017). Characterisation of the indumentum and the laticifers in the leaves and stems of Gomphocarpus physocarpus (Apocynaceae). South African Journal of Botany, 109, 356–357. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2017.01.134
</ref>

The flowers are small, with white hoods and about 1 cm across.  The [[Follicle (fruit)|follicle]] (a type of [[fruit]]) is a pale green, in shape an inflated spheroid, and filled with air. It is covered with rough hairs. It reaches {{cvt|8|cm}} diameter. The leaves are light green, linear to lanceolate and {{cvt|7|–|10|cm}} long, {{cvt|1.2|cm}} broad. The brown seeds have silky tufts.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Llamas |first1=Kirsten Albrecht |title=Tropical Flowering Plants: A Guide to Identification and Cultivation |publisher=Timber Press |year=2003 |isbn=0-88192-585-3 |page=73 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Iremonger |first1=Susan |title=A Guide to the Plants of the Blue Mountains of Jamaica |publisher=The University of West Indies Press |year=2002 |isbn=976-640-031-8 |page=47 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tkTKtH77KpoC&pg=PA47}}</ref>

This plant will readily hybridize with ''[[Gomphocarpus fruticosus]]'' creating intermediate forms.<ref>{{cite book |first1=A. |last1=Gurib-Fakim |chapter=''Gomphocarpus fruticosus'' (L.) W.T.Aiton |chapter-url=http://database.prota.org/PROTAhtml/Gomphocarpus%20fruticosus_En.htm |editor1-last=Schmelzer |editor1-first=G.H. |editor2-last=Gurib-Fakim |editor2-first=A. |title=Prota 11(2): Medicinal plants/Plantes médicinales 2 |publisher=PROTA |location=Wageningen, Netherlands |year=2011 }}</ref>

Other names for the plant include in Afrikaans: balmelkbossie, balbossie, wilde kapok and in Zulu: umbababa, umbemiso, umangwazane, umqumnqwewe, uphuphuma, usingalwesalukazi, umsingalwesalukazi.<ref name="SANBI2010" />

==Ecology==
The plant's stamens are fused to the head of the style and all the pollen of each stamen is within two [[pollinia]]. The pouch-like structure formed by the petals that surrounds the reproductive organs encourages pollinia to stick to the legs or [[proboscis]] of pollinating insects. As a result, the pollen packets are carried from plant to plant. The species is self-incompatible, and these specialised structures support this reproduction.<ref name="SANBI2010">{{cite web |last1=Notten |first1=Alice |title=Gomphocarpus physocarpus E.Mey. |url=https://pza.sanbi.org/gomphocarpus-physocarpus |website=South African National Biodiversity Institute |access-date=1 January 2025}}</ref> 
  
''Gomphocarpus physocarpus'' is a food of the [[caterpillar]]s of ''[[Danaus (genus)|Danaus]]'' [[butterflies]], including the African monarch butterfly (''[[Danaus chrysippus]] orientis''). They store the unpleasant tasting and toxic [[cardenolide]]s from the plants to deter predators. Distinctive colouration alerts predators before they attack.<ref name="SANBI2010" />

== Toxicity ==
The sap produced by the plants is toxic, and if ingested all parts can potentially affect the heart, breathing, central nervous system and the stomach.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Swan Plants - Educational Or Harmful? |url=https://poisons.co.nz/articles-and-info/common-poisons-around-the-garden/view/swan-plants---educational-or-harmful- |access-date=2026-03-29 |website=poisons.co.nz |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Gomphocarpus physocarpus |url=https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/gomphocarpus-physocarpus/ |access-date=2026-03-29 |website=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network |language=en}}</ref> It may also cause eye injuries.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ono |first=Takashi |last2=Kinoshita |first2=Katsuhito |last3=Iwasaki |first3=Takuya |last4=Mori |first4=Yosai |last5=Nejima |first5=Ryohei |last6=Nakamura |first6=Yasuko |last7=Amano |first7=Shiro |last8=Aihara |first8=Makoto |last9=Miyata |first9=Kazunori |date=2019-11-22 |title=Clinical Courses Of Corneal Endothelial Dysfunction Due To Gomphocarpus physocarpus Milky Latex-Induced Injury: A Case Series |url=https://www.dovepress.com/clinical-courses-of-corneal-endothelial-dysfunction-due-to-gomphocarpu-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-OPTH |journal=Clinical Ophthalmology |language=English |volume=13 |pages=2293–2299 |doi=10.2147/OPTH.S230009 |doi-access=free|pmc=6878928 }}</ref> In 2017 a [[Northland Region|Northland, New Zealand]] man was reported to have become temporarily blind after getting sap in his eyes, with one eye still affected nine months later.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Northern Advocate |date=2017-06-08 |title=Swan plant's toxic sap blinds Northland man |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/northern-advocate/news/swan-plants-toxic-sap-blinds-northland-man/3GAK2XZZW37ZMF2OYVPCHNHQ5M/ |access-date=2026-03-29 |work=The New Zealand Herald |language=en-NZ}}</ref>
